questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How Charles Mackay's 1841 book on crowd behavior shaped modern views of speculative manias
The Dutch tulip price bubble of the 1630s, how the tulip trade arose, and how historians view it
The Ottoman origins of the tulip and its spread through European gardens and royal courts
How a mosaic virus created the tulip's prized streaks, and how growers learned to control it
questions.explain: It covers tulip mania, the Dutch tulip business, and debate over how serious the bubble was.

questions.q: Who is largely responsible for spreading tulip bulbs in the late 16th century?
options: Ogier de Busbecq
Nicolas van Wassenaer
Philipp Blom
Carolus Clusius
questions.explain: Botanist Carolus Clusius is largely responsible for the spread of tulip bulbs in the final years of the 16th century.

questions.q: During which months could bulbs be moved and bought on the spot market?
options: June to September
April and May
October to December
January to March
questions.explain: During the dormant phase from June to September bulbs could be uprooted, so spot purchases occurred then.

questions.q: What caused the colorful flame-like streaks on prized tulips?
options: A cold climate during the Little Ice Age
A mosaic virus that breaks the petal colour
Careful crossbreeding by Dutch growers
Soil rich in minerals in Leiden
questions.explain: The effect is produced when bulbs are infected with the tulip breaking virus.

questions.q: Why might traders have been willing to pay high forward prices, according to the passage?
options: The Dutch government guaranteed all forward contracts against default by buyers
Edicts encouraged short selling, which lowered the cost of buying bulbs
Buyers expected bulbs to be scarce over winter, which raised resale value
Contracts could be voided for a small cost, which lowered buyers' risk
questions.explain: The passage says high prices may reflect expectations that contracts could be voided cheaply, and forward contracts were unenforceable.
